topic: Running LLM Commands on ESP32: Embedded AI Agent Hardware

key_points: Runs a 28.9M-parameter LLM on an ESP32-S3 (512KB SRAM, 8MB PSRAM, 16MB flash) at 9.88 tokens/sec end-to-end
Fits the model by storing 25M params in a flash lookup table using Google's Per-Layer Embeddings (from Gemma 3n)
Three-tier memory layout: SRAM for activations/norm weights, PSRAM for core+head, flash for the 25M-param embedding table (~450 bytes sampled per token)
Models: Barista (espresso QA) and TinyStories (story generation), 14.9MB at 4-bit
Model limits: trained on TinyStories, so it won't answer questions, follow instructions, write code, or know facts
Workflow: fetch_model.sh (download/verify) then deploy.sh (compile/flash)
Distributed 56M-parameter LLM inference across three ESP32-S3 boards communicating via ESP-NOW
Split-PLE: the 50.3M-param embedding table split across boards A and B to fit 16MB flash each
Board C hosts WiFi + web server; browser streams generated text via SSE
Board B keeps a 1.5MB KV cache in PSRAM (256 positions) so the transformer attends to the full sequence
Trained on WikiText-103, 4-bit quantized; built on slvDev/esp32-ai's architecture
Shows how to scale past a single board's flash limits
Runs a 180.9M-parameter LLM/SLM on the ESP32-P4 (WT9932P4-Tiny board, ~$6-10) at about 9 tokens/sec
Uses PLE-MoE-W1.58A8 architecture: mixed ternary, Q8, and FP16 storage totaling ~44 MiB across flash and PSRAM
ESP32-P4 is far more capable than the S3: XespV acceleration (up to 30x speedup), supports up to 32MB PSRAM, 400MHz
MoE weights in PSRAM, PLE weights in flash via XIP, cache/working memory in DIRAM
Has early Instruct (ChatML) and Agent capabilities, though unstable
Weights transferred over USB at startup; give it an SD card and it can run fully offline
Early proof that a tiny LLM can run on ESP32: 260K-param tinyllamas checkpoint (karpathy/tinyllamas) on TinyStories
Uses llama2.c (karpathy) with optimizations for the ESP32
Achieves 19.13 tok/s via dual-core math, ESP-DSP SIMD dot products, 240MHz CPU / 80MHz PSRAM overclock, larger instruction cache
Even a small model needs ~1MB RAM; used LILYGO T-Camera S3 (8MB PSRAM + screen)
Conclusion: possible but 'not very useful' for real tasks at this scale
Realtime Voice AI on ESP32 backed by Cloudflare Durable Objects + Workers AI (Deepgram STT/TTS)
100+ Voice AI models; Secure WebSockets & Edge Functions for >20-minute uninterrupted conversations
Cloud-only approach contrasts with fully-on-device inference — the 'agent' path for command-style interaction
Alternative: local-ai-toys project supports local LLMs/TTS (Qwen, Mistral) via MLX on ESP32 devices
Covers both the cloud-assisted and fully-local agent hardware spectrum

stats.fact: An ESP32-S3 can run a 28.9M-parameter LLM fully on-device at 9.88 tokens/sec, with 25M params stored in flash using Google's Per-Layer Embeddings.
The ESP32-S3 offers only 512KB SRAM, but up to 8MB PSRAM and 16MB flash — memory, not compute, is the binding constraint for embedded LLMs.
The 180.9M-parameter PFor model runs on an ESP32-P4 at ~9 tokens/sec using PLE-MoE with W1.58A8 quantization, occupying ~44MiB across flash and PSRAM.
The ESP32-P4 supports up to 32MB PSRAM and a 400MHz clock, with XespV hardware acceleration delivering up to 30x speedup — a major upgrade over the ESP32-S3.
A 56M-parameter LLM can be split across three ESP32-S3 boards (via ESP-NOW, Split-PLE, and a 1.5MB KV cache) to exceed single-board flash limits.
The simplest on-device ESP32 LLM (260K params, tinyllamas) hits 19.13 tok/s after dual-core + ESP-DSP SIMD optimization of llama2.c.
Fully on-device models trained on TinyStories cannot answer questions, follow instructions, write code, or recall facts — real agent/command behavior requires either a bigger chip or a cloud model.
Cloud-assisted voice AI on ESP32 (Cloudflare Durable Objects + Deepgram) supports 100+ voice models and >20-minute uninterrupted conversations.

angles: Memory-tier architecture: how Per-Layer Embeddings squeeze a 25M-param table into flash and only sample ~450 bytes per token
Chip comparison: ESP32-S3 (affordable, ~512KB SRAM) vs ESP32-P4 (32MB PSRAM, XespV acceleration, agent-capable)
The agent tradeoff: fully-on-device SLMs can't do real instruction-following, so command execution needs cloud (WebSockets) or distributed multi-board setups
Scaling tricks: 4-bit/W1.58 quantization, KV cache in PSRAM, Split-PLE across boards, ESP-NOW distributed inference
Practical workflow: fetch_model.sh + deploy.sh, ESP-IDF build & flash, choosing a board with PSRAM + flash headroom
Realistic expectations: 9-20 tok/s is fine for voice replies and command recognition, not for code generation or factual Q&A
